cards.back: Common pop progressions: I-V-vi-IV (four-chord loop), I-IV-V (rock/blues), ii-V-I (jazz cadence) — each creates a different harmonic character.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chords and Accompaniment Writing
cards.back: Accompaniment styles define genre: Alberti bass (Classical), riff (rock/pop), broken chords (Romantic), ostinato (minimalist), pedal/drone (folk/traditional).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chords and Accompaniment Writing
cards.back: Harmonic rhythm (how often chords change) affects momentum: fast harmonic rhythm creates drive; slow harmonic rhythm creates stasis and calm.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Chords and Accompaniment Writing
cards.back: Dominant seventh chords (V7) create tension that resolves to the tonic — they are essential for cadences and key-defining progressions.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Choose genre-appropriate progressions. Match accompaniment style to genre. Use cadences intentionally. Notate chord symbols. Annotate harmonic decisions.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: You just put chords over the melody and it sounds fine. Correct: Chord choices and accompaniment patterns must be INTENTIONAL and GENRE-APPROPRIATE. Classical styles use functional harmony with cadences; popular styles use stock progressions and riffs; folk styles use drones and modal harmony. cards.front: Exam Technique for Chords and Accompaniment Writing Questions
cards.back: In the AQA GCSE Music listening exam, questions about chords and accompaniment writing typically ask you to: identify features by ear; describe how they are used; explain their effect; compare features between extracts. The key to success is precise terminology — never use vague language.
